description: I am a PhD researcher in molecular & POC diagnostics. My work is turning noisy biological signals into a result a non-specialist can act on. Join if you want a teammate who brings the clinical side and does the unglamorous work. Looking for front-end/UI devs, time-series or ML on physiological data, a designer, and anyone into space medicine or human factors. Beginners welcome. Please provide your contact info.
summary:
When astronauts venture beyond Earth, even a minor health issue can become a mission-critical challenge. Millions of kilometres from immediate medical support, with communication delays that limit real-time assistance, crews must be able to monitor their health, recognize risks, and make informed decisions independently. Making human exploration of the Moon and Mars sustainable requires more than getting astronauts there; it requires keeping them healthy.
BioOrbit aims to address this challenge through an offline-first health monitoring app designed for astronauts on the Moon, Mars, and beyond. On a tablet, crew members can access an interactive 3D human body displaying health status, habitat conditions (air quality, noise, and radiation), and trend charts comparing personal readings against pre-flight baselines.
The app tracks key health indicators, including blood pressure, heart rate, blood glucose, temperature, sleep, mood, respiratory rate, and radiation exposure. It adapts to four environments: transit spacecraft, space stations, rovers, and surface bases. Alerts use NASA-STD-3001 limits and a space-adapted early-warning score, providing clear, actionable guidance.
Thresholds and expected in-flight changes are informed by NASA standards, Human Research Program evidence, and crew data from NASA’s Open Science Data Repository. All prototype data is simulated; BioOrbit is a decision-support tool, not a medical device.
details:
What it does

BioOrbit is a crew health console for long missions beyond Earth. It helps each astronaut answer two questions: "Am I OK?" and "What should I do next?"

  • Interactive 3D body map. A 3D astronaut model with 6 body regions (brain and mind, heart and circulation, lungs and breathing, blood and immune, stomach and nutrition, whole body and exposure). Regions with data light up in their alert colour; hovering or tapping one shows its latest readings.
  • Personal baselines first. Core indicators (heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep and mood) appear next to the astronaut’s own pre-flight reference, not only a population range.
  • The cabin in the same view. CO₂ and O₂ partial pressure, total cabin pressure, temperature. Other parameters include humidity, noise, dust, radiation, combustion products, water supply and solar-storm presence, alongside crew locations by cabin zone. Many symptoms (headache, poor sleep, irritated eyes) start in the cabin, not the body.
  • Trends. 24-hour, 7-day and 30-day charts with personal pre-flight reference bands, exact values on tap, and visible gaps where data is missing. Other measures are shown hourly, and sleep is shown by mission day.
  • Alerts with a plan. Four tiers: Advisory, Caution, Warning and Emergency. Each alert shows why it fired, the recorded evidence, step-by-step guidance from our measurement workbook, and a recheck deadline. The crew acknowledge an alert to record their review; it steps down one tier only after three normal readings.
  • Crew check-ins. A crew member can record vital signs, consciousness level, oxygen use, headache severity and 13 symptoms such as chest pain, breathlessness at rest, new confusion or vision change. Reports are saved in mission time and evaluated at once; red flags such as new confusion raise an Emergency immediately.
  • Four mission environments. Each mission run is set as a transit spacecraft, space station, rover or surface base, and the rules adapt: the daily radiation reference is 1.3 mSv/day in free space and 0.9 mSv/day on a planetary surface, and lunar or Martian dust checks apply only on the surface.
  • Research pages. A landing page, 13 chapters of biology documentation, a searchable atlas of 87 measurements, a glossary, and a searchable library of the 139 references behind the project.

How it works

BioOrbit has three parts, all in the public GitHub repository:

  • Simulator (Python standard library). Creates astronauts with personal profiles and pre-flight observations, back-fills history, streams live astronaut and cabin data, and schedules abnormal scenarios such as a solar storm, hypoxia, cabin pressure loss or post-spacewalk symptoms. It keeps its clock and delivery journal in SQLite, so it can resume after an interruption and resend safely. Every value is labelled synthetic.
  • Backend (Django and PostgreSQL). Validates every event against the shared event contract (units, identities and values), stores accepted events with their original payloads, updates current readings, and evaluates the alert rules in mission-time order inside one transaction. Read APIs serve the dashboard, trends and alerts; check-ins use signed-in sessions with CSRF protection.
  • Frontend (React 19, Vite and Three.js). The crew console, 3D body map, charts and check-in form, with light and dark themes and reduced-motion support.

The rule engine is driven by our measurement workbook: 83 indicators (88 data fields), each with its Earth reference, expected value in space, device, collection cadence and alert triggers. Acute vital signs are scored with NEWS2 (Royal College of Physicians), adjusted for known in-flight shifts such as lower blood pressure, a lower resting heart rate and a higher core temperature, judged against each astronaut’s own in-flight band. Eight pattern rules link signals across body and cabin: for example, a headache or short sleep while the 7-day CO₂ average reaches 2.5 mmHg points to the cabin first, and joint pain or tingling within 24 hours of a spacewalk opens a decompression check. Missing inputs stay "not evaluated", never "normal", and overdue data appears as a collection task, separate from medical alerts.

How we used NASA data

  • NASA-STD-3001 Volumes 1 and 2 and 18 OCHMO technical briefs set the hard limits and response prompts: cabin CO₂ (7-day average 2.5 mmHg, 1-hour 3 mmHg), the inspired O₂ floor, cabin pressure, noise, dust and drinking water, and radiation (600 mSv career limit; 250 mSv design limit per solar particle event).
  • NASA Human Research Program pages and evidence reports (five hazards, human system risks) shaped what we monitor and how the body regions are grouped.
  • 22 NASA Technical Reports Server documents set the monitoring rhythm and inputs: ISS acoustics flight rules and noise data, the Reaction Self Test, SANS eye surveillance, standard measures, EVA injury evidence, surface EVA health, kidney-stone risk, bone metabolism, Earth-Independent Medical Operations and clinical decision support.
  • NASA Life Sciences Portal standard measures informed which crew measures to collect, and how often.
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR). We pulled all 121 Homo sapiens studies through the OSDR API and catalogued 41 relevant ones in the app’s reference library. We analysed the Inspiration4 clinical panels (OSD-569 blood counts, OSD-575 serum chemistry and cytokines, OSD-656 urine inflammation): the day after landing, all four crew had higher glucose (+24%), CRP (+48%) and monocyte share (+25%), and lower white cells (−15%) and neutrophils (−13%) than before flight. With four people and a three-day flight, we use these findings as research context, not as thresholds.

Space Agency Partner data

CSA’s Bio-Monitor smart garment and radiation pages shaped our wearable and dosimeter assumptions. ESA’s telemedicine work and the Tempus Pro vital-signs monitor, which ESA tested in Antarctica, set the vital-sign channels and ranges we simulate.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Crew autonomy. Near Mars, a message to Earth can take up to about 22 minutes each way, and evacuation is impossible. In January 2026, NASA’s Crew-11 came home early in the first medical evacuation from the ISS; beyond low Earth orbit that option does not exist.
  • Earlier detection. Comparing each reading with the astronaut’s own baseline catches drift before a value crosses a population limit.
  • Calmer, clearer alerts. The cabin is checked before the person, alerts do not flicker on and off (three normal readings to step down), and missing data is never treated as normal.
  • On Earth. The same design fits Antarctic stations, ships, submarines and remote clinics, wherever help is far away.

What makes it creative

  • The 3D body is the main interface, not decoration, and the cabin sits around it, so body and environment are read together.
  • Personal baseline first, then the expected value in space, then the clinical limit.
  • Every alert explains itself: its evidence, the rule’s condition, guidance and a recheck time travel with it.
  • Honest by design: unknown values show "—", gaps stay gaps, simulated fixtures are labelled, and nothing is invented.
  • One console for four mission environments.

Factors we considered

  • Safety. The app suggests checks, never a diagnosis or a drug dose. Thresholds that are not NASA limits are marked as ours and need flight-surgeon review.
  • Mission time versus real time. Accelerated simulations judge data freshness by mission time, separately from the live feed’s receipt age.
  • Accessibility. Light and dark themes, reduced motion, tier names beside colours, and keyboard-reachable chart values.
  • No NASA branding. BioOrbit is an independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

Current limits and next steps

Real wearables and spacecraft sensors are not connected yet, the simulator is not a validated physiological model. Next: connect a smart garment, a Tempus Pro-class monitor and dosimeters, run the full stack on board, and test it in Earth analogs.

Tools and technologies

Python 3 (simulator, standard library only), Django, PostgreSQL with psycopg, SQLite, JSON Schema event contracts, React 19, Vite, Three.js, Lucide icons, DM Sans and Space Grotesk fonts (Google Fonts), Docker and Docker Compose, Netlify (website hosting), Cloudflare Tunnel (demo backend) and GitHub.
